enonce_markdown:
In insurance, the person who takes out a policy and pays the premium is called the:

a) insurer

b) underwriter

c) loss adjuster

d) insured
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In an insurance contract there are two parties: the insurer (the company that accepts the risk) and the insured (the person who is protected).

### Solution

The insurer and the underwriter are on the company's side, and a loss adjuster examines claims for the insurer. The one who pays the premium and receives protection is the **insured**.

**Answer: d.**

enonce_markdown:
The regular payment that an insured person makes to the insurance company for cover is called a:

a) claim

b) premium

c) policy

d) indemnity
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Key insurance words: premium = the price of cover; claim = the request for payment after a loss; policy = the written contract; indemnity = the compensation.

### Solution

The money paid for the cover is the **premium**. The claim is the request made after a loss, the policy is the contract and the indemnity is what the insurer pays out.

**Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown:
Mr Tabi insures the stock of his shop against fire for 8 000 000 FCFA. A fire destroys part of the stock, whose value at the time was 3 500 000 FCFA. Under the principle of indemnity, the **maximum** the insurer will pay is:

a) 3 500 000 FCFA

b) 4 500 000 FCFA

c) 8 000 000 FCFA

d) 11 500 000 FCFA
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Indemnity means the insured is restored to the position he was in just before the loss, no better and no worse. Compensation cannot exceed the actual loss or the sum insured.

### Solution

Actual loss = 3 500 000 FCFA; sum insured = 8 000 000 FCFA. The insurer pays the smaller amount, so **3 500 000 FCFA**. Paying 8 000 000 FCFA would give Mr Tabi a profit of 4 500 000 FCFA from the fire, which indemnity forbids. 11 500 000 FCFA is the sum of the two amounts and has no meaning.

**Answer: a.**

enonce_markdown:
Insurable interest is required in an insurance contract. In which of the following cases is there **no** insurable interest?

a) A farmer insuring his own harvested crops

b) A man insuring the life of his wife

c) A man insuring the shop of a stranger he has never met

d) A company insuring the life of its managing director
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Insurable interest means the insured would suffer a financial loss if the thing insured were damaged or the person died. Without it, the contract is a bet and is void.

### Solution

The farmer owns the crops (a), a husband depends financially on his wife (b), and the company would lose if its director died (d). The man in (c) would lose nothing if the stranger's shop burned, so he has **no insurable interest**.

**Answer: c.**

choix.texte: A farmer insuring his own harvested crops
A man insuring the life of his wife
A man insuring the shop of a stranger he has never met
A company insuring the life of its managing director

enonce_markdown:
A warehouse in Douala is insured against **fire only**. During a heavy storm, lightning strikes and the warehouse catches fire, and the goods inside are burned. On another occasion, floods from the same storm soak and spoil goods in a second, identical warehouse insured on the same terms.

Using the principle of **proximate cause**, state whether each claim will be paid and explain why.

(6 marks)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The proximate cause is the nearest, effective and dominant cause of the loss. The insurer pays only if that cause is a risk covered by the policy.

### Solution

**Introduction.** Proximate cause means the insurer looks for the main cause that actually produced the loss, not a distant cause.

**First warehouse.** The goods were burned. The proximate cause is **fire**, even though lightning started it. Fire is covered by the policy, so the claim **will be paid**, up to the actual loss (indemnity).

**Second warehouse.** The goods were spoiled by **flood water**. Flood is not covered by a fire-only policy, so the claim **will not be paid**, although the storm is the same.

**Conclusion.** The same storm gives two different results because the cause that directly produced the damage was covered in one case and not in the other.

(3 marks for each warehouse: decision 1, proximate cause 1, explanation 1.)

enonce_markdown:
Madame Ewane owns a boutique. The stock was worth 10 000 000 FCFA, but she insured it for only 6 000 000 FCFA against fire, under a policy containing an **average clause**. A fire destroyed goods worth 2 000 000 FCFA.

(a) Calculate the compensation she will receive.

(b) Explain why she will not receive the full 2 000 000 FCFA, and state what she should have done.

(c) Explain how the principle of utmost good faith applies when she first fills in the proposal form.

(8 marks)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Under-insurance is penalised by the average clause: compensation = (sum insured / value at risk) x loss. Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei) requires the proposer to disclose every material fact.

### Solution

**(a) Calculation** (3 marks)

Compensation = (sum insured / value of stock) x loss
= (6 000 000 / 10 000 000) x 2 000 000
= 0.6 x 2 000 000 = **1 200 000 FCFA**.

**(b) Explanation** (2.5 marks)

She insured only 60% of the stock (**under-insurance**), so she is considered to bear the other 40% of the risk herself and bears 40% of the loss: 800 000 FCFA. She should have insured the stock for its full value, 10 000 000 FCFA, and updated the sum insured when prices or stock levels rose.

**(c) Utmost good faith** (2.5 marks)

In the proposal form she must declare honestly every material fact that could affect the insurer's decision to accept the risk or the premium, for example the real value of the stock, the building materials, the presence of fire extinguishers, and any earlier fires. If she hides or falsifies a fact, the contract becomes voidable and the insurer may refuse to pay a claim.
